name: Legionarii Herculiani seniores (palatina)

abilities.name: Testudo
abilities.text: The troops of this unit raise their shields above their heads in a defensive formation.

abilities.name: Spear Wall
abilities.text: The unit moves into close wall formation.

abilities.name: Square
abilities.text: The unit moves into a close square formation. Note that it cannot move whilst this ability is active.

abilities.name: Shield Screen
abilities.text: The unit raises their shields in a static defensive formation.

abilities.name: Use the Whip
abilities.text: Improved defence and fatigue resistance for a short time at the cost of overexertion.

attributes.name: Disciplined
attributes.text: This unit does not suffer a morale penalty when the general dies. It can also rally after routing more often.

attributes.name: Encourage
attributes.text: This unit provides a morale bonus to nearby allies.

attributes.name: Hide (forest)
attributes.text: This unit can hide in forests until enemy units get too close.

attributes.name: Formation Attack
attributes.text: The unit will try to stay in formation when in melee.

attributes.name: Immune to Fear
attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: The Jovians and Herculians were the most famous units of the late Roman army. Ammianus Marcellinus, Vegetius, Eunapius, Zosimus, and Gregory of Tours - all mention them. The names of these units indicate that they were formed from soldiers of the Iovia and Herculia legions, created during the first Tetrarchy. However, there is another version of the emergence of the Jovians and Herculians. According to the statement of Vegetius, both legions were formed in the 3rd century AD in Illyricum, apparently before Diocletian came to power. At their formation they were named Martiobarbuli and numbered 6,000 soldiers each. This name was given to these legions because the legionaries were armed with martiobarbuli or plumbatas. The legionaries carried five of these throwing darts inside their shields (Veg., I, 17). The Martiobarbuli proved themselves in many wars and already in their time became the most illustrious legions of the Late Empire. After Diocletian elected Maximian as his co-emperor (286), it was customary to call the most distinguished military units Jovian and Herculian (Aur. Viet., Caes., 39, 18), so the Martiobarbuli were renamed Jovians and Herculians. These glorious legions were preferred by many Emperors to other units of the field army (Veg., I, 17). According to historians R. Scharf and E.A. Mekhamadiev, the terms seniores and iuniores reflected the process of gradual division of the late Roman legions, when from the ranks of the older legions, designated as seniores, were separated new units called iuniores.
history: In the face of an increasing number of barbarian incursions, the effective defence of Rome’s now-sprawling territory became a serious problem in the 4th century AD. The Emperor Constantine’s controversial solution was to divide the army into two halves. 'Limitanei', literally ‘the men on the limes’ or 'borders', were frontier garrison troops intended to pin down an invading force until the full-time 'comitatenses', the late-Roman equivalent of the traditional Legionaries, could arrive to deal with the situation decisively. Although well-equipped, limitanei were generally considered by all to be second-class warriors. This was possibly because they were often part-time soldiers who had been encouraged to settle and farm the land around their outposts in exchange for policing the Empire's borders.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
